text: Picture this: you present a model's accuracy on Monday. On Thursday your manager reruns your notebook and gets a slightly different number. Or a teammate clones your project, and it crashes on their laptop. Neither of you did anything wrong on purpose — the analysis simply wasn't reproducible. It depended on randomness, library versions, file locations, or data that nobody wrote down. Reproducibility means someone else, or you six months from now, can rerun your work and get the exact same result — the last habit in our reliable-code chapter, and it costs only a few lines.

Computers generate pseudo-random numbers from a starting value called a seed — same seed, same sequence, every time. NumPy's recommended approach creates a generator with an explicit seed. Create two generators both seeded with 42, draw three normal values from each, and they agree exactly — array equal returns True. Create two more generators with no seed at all, and they almost never agree. The number 42 has no special meaning whatsoever — pick any integer you like, and just keep using it.

Randomness also hides inside pandas and scikit-learn, and both take a random underscore state argument. Sample three rows with random underscore state equals 42, and on a ten-row illustrative table, you get the exact same three order IDs back every single run. Split a DataFrame into train and test sets the same way, and the split comes out identical every time too. Get in the habit of setting random underscore state everywhere you split, sample, shuffle, or train a model that leans on randomness.

The exact same code can behave differently across library versions, so record exactly what you used. Create a virtual environment for each project with python dash m venv dot venv, then capture what's installed with python dash m pip freeze, redirected into requirements dot txt. A teammate recreates that identical environment later with pip install dash r requirements dot txt. Commit that file right next to your code, and note your Python version in your README too.

A hard-coded path like C colon slash Users slash alex slash Desktop slash orders dot csv works on exactly one computer in the entire world. Build paths relative to the script instead — Path of dunder-file, resolved, gives you the folder the script itself lives in, and you build every other path, like your raw data file, from that root. The project then works correctly wherever it gets cloned, on anyone's machine.

The hashlib sha256 line produces a 64-character fingerprint of a file's exact bytes. If the raw data changes by even a single character, that fingerprint changes completely. Print it, or save it right alongside your results, and you can prove exactly which version of the data produced them. Also treat raw data as read-only — cleaning code should read from one folder and write its output to a different one, never overwriting the original file.

Here's the checklist to actually follow. Seed every random step, and record the seed you used. Pin your library versions in requirements dot txt. Use relative paths built with pathlib, never hard-coded ones. Keep raw data completely untouched, and fingerprint it. And restart and run everything from scratch, one more time, before you ever share it with anyone.

To recap: seeds make randomness repeatable, pinned requirements make environments repeatable, relative paths make projects portable, and fingerprints make data traceable. Put all four together, and your Thursday number finally matches your Monday number. Next comes the Capstone, where we use everything from this entire course on one real dataset, end to end.
